editorNote: August’s home-computer magazines put Lucasfilm games, optical discs and dial-up communities in the spotlight.
morningLine: A movie studio takes the joystick; the neighborhood bulletin board grows up.

lead.headline: Lucasfilm brings the movie studio’s flair to Atari game screens
lead.dek: Ballblazer and Rescue on Fractalus bring split-screen sport and mountain rescue to the Atari disk drive.
body: Lucasfilm’s long-awaited Atari games receive an enthusiastic examination in the August Antic. Michael Ciraolo reviews Ballblazer and Rescue on Fractalus, distributed by Epyx, at $40 apiece for 48K Atari disk systems. These are this month’s review-room attractions, not newly dated launches for the week.

Ballblazer makes a sporting arena out of the computer screen. Two players—or one against the machine—steer Rotofoils in split-screen perspective, driving a Plasmorb toward moving goalbeams. Longer successful shots are worth more, inviting a choice between a safe approach and a spectacular attempt from farther out.

Rescue on Fractalus turns the monitor into a cockpit above fractal-generated mountains. Stranded pilots await collection amid enemy saucers and gun emplacements; instruments, footsteps and the knock at the airlock help give the rescue mission its character. The mountainous view is part of the action, not merely scenery behind it.

The route to official disks has not been smooth. Antic recalls a year of anticipation, buggy bootlegs and legal battles without identifying litigants. Its review also reports that initial disks worked only with Atari 810 and 1050 drives; the problem was corrected, and Epyx promised replacements for nonworking copies. Buyers should distinguish that corrected distribution trouble from the games themselves.

stories.headline: Atari puts an encyclopedia on an optical disc
body: Atari’s Summer CES demonstration put an unlikely companion beside the 520ST: a CD-ROM prototype carrying an encyclopedia. August COMPUTE! reports that Activenture of Pacific Grove was developing the software, and that a 23-volume, nine-million-word encyclopedia with its index occupied only a quarter of the disc.

The demonstration points beyond the usual floppy-disk library. Full-information indexing could make a reference work searchable in ways paper cannot easily match. Activenture engineering vice president Tom Rolander also raised a less technical question: what would households pay for information when it no longer arrived as a shelf of handsome books?

Atari hoped for availability late in 1985 or early in 1986 at about $500. That is a forecast, not a retail offer. The encyclopedia publisher remained unnamed while its contract was unfinished; the working show prototype is the news, not a promised machine already on store shelves.

stories.headline: The ST’s next test is software, not specifications
body: A new Atari ST needs more than specifications to win a place on the desk. Michael Ciraolo’s August Antic software report surveys developers working toward the programs that could give the machine its daily purpose.

Stoneware announced an agreement with Atari for an unnamed filing program, with user-selectable colors, fonts and file layouts. Microbits Peripheral Products was developing Omega for both ST and 8-bit Ataris, using icons, windows and pull-down menus controlled by mouse or joystick. Expected prices were roughly $50 for the 16-bit version and $10 less for the 8-bit edition.

Spinnaker said eight ST products were planned for fall. Infocom expected its text-adventure line on the machine but supplied no release date, while Ken Williams said Sierra On-Line would bring King’s Quest and Ultima II. These are development plans to watch, not an inventory of programs available this week.

stories.headline: A construction set for the neighborhood bulletin board
body: Scott Brause, sysop of the Jersey Atari Computer Group, spent two years developing the Bulletin Board Construction Set after frustrations with AMIS and FOREM. Eric Clausen’s August Antic review describes a 48K machine-language system whose four editors handle configuration, menus and polls, user logs and message bases.

BBCS offers up to 26 menus with 30 entries each, as many as 257 online messages and 1,940-byte individual messages. Support for 1200 baud, XMODEM and ASCII transfers, terminal definitions and remote housekeeping gives a club board room to grow beyond a single local circle.

Clausen also found memory and DOS compatibility issues, editor bugs in version 1.0 and preliminary documentation in need of rewriting. Antic disclosed that its own marketing director had acquired the program for the magazine’s catalog. The useful new tools and that commercial interest both belong in the account.

storeShelves.label: Top 5 Computer Games — editorial reviews and previews, not sales rankings
items: Ballblazer — Epyx/Lucasfilm, Atari 48K disk, $40; split-screen futuristic ball sport. Reviewed this month, not proven newly released this week.
Rescue on Fractalus — Epyx/Lucasfilm, Atari 48K disk, $40; fractal-terrain rescue flight action.
Adventure Master — CBS Software, Atari 48K disk, $44.95; menu-driven adventure authoring, two disks, graphics editor and sample/unfinished adventures.
Maxwell Manor — Avalon Hill, Atari 48K disk, $25; more than 50 screens, ten skill levels and over 100 maze variations in Antic’s review.
The Eidolon — Lucasfilm Atari game listed in Epyx’s forthcoming slate, not verified on sale this week.

briefs.headline: Assembly lessons arrive by modem
briefs.summary: August Antic describes Chris Crawford’s eight-month 6502 assembly course on ANTIC ONLINE/CompuServe, begun in mid-June with monthly lessons; WUN directory had over 130 users groups.

briefs.headline: BBS culture grows beyond the hobby shop
briefs.summary: Martin Lasden’s August 4 New York Times report says CompuServe reported over 200,000 subscribers, up about 70% in a year; Mike Cane estimated at least 2,500 home bulletin boards. Attribute numbers; not a new August 12 census.

market.headline: Software and services compete for the home-computer dollar
market.summary: Developers are promising ST programs while established Atari owners gain games and board software. Online charges remain part of the budget: August Antic quotes Delphi at $6 an hour at either 300 or 1200 baud, and CompuServe at $6 and $7.75 respectively.

worldAnchor.headline: Japan Air Lines jumbo jet crashes on domestic flight
worldAnchor.summary: Japan Air Lines Flight 123 crashed in mountainous Gunma Prefecture on August 12 during its Tokyo–Osaka flight. Of 524 aboard, four survived; 520 died.

bbsNote.headline: Sysops get new tools while services compete on hourly cost
bbsNote.summary: August Antic’s Telecomputers 85 issue supplies a substantial dated online beat; these are reported features and prices, not fabricated BBS messages.

posts.text: Scott Brause’s 48K machine-language construction set supports configurable boards, remote maintenance and 1200-baud transfers. Review names beta sysop Eric Semel and Michigan Atari Computer Enthusiasts.

Antic quotes Delphi at $6/hour for 300 or 1200 baud versus CompuServe $6 at 300 and $7.75 at 1200. The article’s free subscription/hour promotion explicitly applied to July only: do not advertise it as live in August.
An August COMPUTE! advertisement promotes menu mode for beginners and prompt/command modes for experienced users, with compose, edit, send and file functions. Treat ease-of-use claims as advertising.
Chris Crawford’s monthly 6502 course and the WUN club directory turn dial-up time into instruction and user-group coordination.

curiosity.headline: Nine million words—and the disc is still mostly empty
curiosity.summary: Atari’s optical-disc demonstration makes printed encyclopedias look physically extravagant.
curiosity.detail: August COMPUTE! reports Activenture had put a 23-volume, nine-million-word encyclopedia plus index on a disc that remained three-quarters empty. This was a Summer CES prototype report, not a new product shipped this week. Rolander discussed how consumers might value the same information without a shelf of books.
